title: Non-Abelian Gauge Field Mechanics
authors: Ivan Velkovsky, Carlos Camacho, Tomoki Ozawa, Hannah Price, Bryce Gadway
abstract: Non-Abelian gauge fields play a key role in describing the behavior of particles whose motion is coupled to internal degrees of freedom, such as their spin. Here, we experimentally realize a tuneable non-Abelian gauge field in an active mechanical lattice by using pairs of oscillators to encode a local pseudo-spin for each site, with inter-site spin-dependent couplings engineered via real-time measurement and feedback. We experimentally extract Wilson-loop observables in our set-up and hence demonstrate that we can create a genuinely non-Abelian gauge field. We then exploit the controllability of our mechanical lattice to engineer non-reciprocal hoppings to explore non-Hermitian non-Abelian gauge potentials. For a two-dimensional (2D) lattice, we demonstrate that the non-Hermiticity can manifest in direction-dependent Wilson loops for a single plaquette, while for a one-dimensional (1D) system, we show that a non-Abelian gauge potential can switch the localization of non-Hermitian skin modes between opposite ends of a chain. Our work establishes active mechanical lattices as a flexible and programmable platform for probing non-Abelian gauge fields and exploring their interplay with non-Hermitian dynamics.
summary: The research demonstrates the ability to create and control non-Abelian gauge fields in a programmable platform built from active mechanical oscillators. By measuring Wilson loops and engineering non-Hermitian couplings, the authors prove genuine non-Abelian behavior and explore related phenomena like mode localization switching.
main_problem: The goal is to experimentally realize and study genuinely non-Abelian gauge fields, and subsequently explore their interplay with non-Hermitian dynamics.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the creation of a tuneable non-Abelian gauge field using mechanical oscillators and showed that non-Hermiticity leads to direction-dependent Wilson loops in 2D and mode localization switching in 1D.
method: The experiment uses an active mechanical lattice where local pseudo-spins are encoded by pairs of coupled classical oscillators. Gauge fields and hoppings are engineered using real-time measurement and feedback control.
model_or_system: The system is a programmable active mechanical lattice simulating spin-1/2 particles hopping on lattices (square or 1D). The dynamics are governed by Hamiltonians parameterized by gauge potentials, allowing for non-reciprocal couplings to explore non-Hermitian physics.
key_observables: Wilson loop observables ($W_i$), which diagnose the Abelian vs. non-Abelian nature of the field; and the left-right localization bias ($B$) in 1D systems.
important_parameters: Coupling amplitudes ($\alpha,  eta$); tuning angles ($	heta_R, 	heta_L$); and the ability to engineer non-reciprocal hoppings.
main_assumptions: The experiment operates in a classical regime, and sources of error include incomplete energy transfer during coupling links.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the measurement of Wilson loop magnitudes ($|W|$), comparing numerical simulations with experimental results for both Abelian and non-Abelian regimes. Another figure shows the measurable left-right bias ($B$) in 1D systems, confirming control over non-Hermitian skin modes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the platform's capability to generate a non-Abelian field via Wilson loop measurements on a 2D lattice. It then extends this control to engineer non-reciprocal hoppings, demonstrating distinct signatures of non-Hermiticity in both 2D and 1D systems.
why_interesting: This work provides an unprecedented physical realization of abstract concepts from high-energy physics (non-Abelian gauge fields) using macroscopic mechanical oscillators, making it highly relevant for experimental quantum simulation techniques.

Each oscillator consists of a mass with a small dipole magnet suspended by springs between a pair of anti-Helmholtz coils. The current through these coils, and hence the force exerted on the masses, is determined dynamically through real-time feedback and measurement via an embedded accelerometer. Using these forces, we can map the hopping of phonons in our mechanical lattice to the dynamics of a particle moving under the Hamiltonian in Eq. 1.
